extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, policy researchers, and the interested public seeking guidance on Canadian patent subject-matter law
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and interpretive criteria used in Canadian law to determine whether a claimed invention qualifies as patentable subject matter (statutory categories, exclusions, and key case-law/office guidance). Covers definitions of the five statutory categories, notable exclusions, and leading cases and office practice affecting eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core patentability prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: An item must fulfill the requirements of novelty, non-obviousness and utility to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if novelty, non-obviousness and utility are satisfied, the claimed subject matter may still be invalid if it does not fall within one of the statutory categories of 'invention' under the Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'invention' (s.2 Patent Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A]ny new and useful art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement in any art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory list defines the categories of patentable subject matter in Canada and is the starting point for all subject-matter eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'art' has been defined broadly as the application of knowledge to effect a desired result; alternatively defined more narrowly as 'an act or series of acts performed by some physical agent upon some physical object and producing in such object some change either of character or of condition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have offered both broad and narrower constructions; context and purposive interpretation will determine whether a claimed practice qualifies as an 'art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is the application of a method to a material or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process may be patentable even if it does not produce a patentable product. However, the Supreme Court of Canada concluded in Tennessee Eastman that medical or therapeutic methods are not contemplated in the definition of 'invention' as a kind of process (i.e., methods of medical treatment are excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is the mechanical embodiment of any function or mode of operation designed to accomplish a particular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Canadian Intellectual Property Office (MOPOP) guidance describes 'machine' as a mechanical embodiment; claim construction must show the claimed subject matter fits within this understanding to be a 'machine.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture implies a product made by hand, by machine, industrially, by mass production and so forth, by changing the character or condition of material objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court in Harvard College v. Canada held that higher life forms (e.g., genetically altered mice) did not fall within 'manufacture.' Whether a claimed product is a 'manufacture' depends on whether it is a product produced by changing material objects' character or condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Composition of matter' is a combination of ingredients or substances – a solid, gas, or fluid – as a chemical union or a physical mixture; taken to include enzymes, reproducible modified genes, and the cells that carry them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish lower from higher life forms for this category (Harvard). Where an invention is a combination of elements, the elements must produce something more than the mere sum of their individual effects—if each element functions independently with no common result, there is no inventive composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new and useful improvement in any art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter is an 'invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most inventions are improvements. Examples: a newfound medical use for a known and patented pharmaceutical compound may qualify as an improvement in an art; eliminating an element from a previously patented composition that results in a new and useful improvement may also be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject matter — scientific principles and abstract theorems (s.27(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 27(8) of the Patent Act: 'No patent shall be granted for any mere scientific principle or abstract theorem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the only explicit statutory exclusion. Practical applications of scientific principles or abstract theorems are not excluded; e.g., a theory is unpatentable but a practical device applying the theory may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded/limited subject matter — higher life forms (Harvard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Harvard College v. Canada (Commissioner of Patents), the Supreme Court (5–4) found that the categories 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter' did not cover higher life forms and upheld the Commissioner's rejection of oncomice claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority framed this as a policy issue requiring explicit legislative direction. The decision has been criticized for the difficulty of drawing a logical line between lower and higher life forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection via components (Monsanto/Schmeiser nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monsanto Canada Inc. v. Schmeiser found that patent claims directed to a modified gene and the cells containing it were patentable and that growing a crop containing those genes could infringe even if a patent for the higher life form per se was not claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a practical pathway to protect higher life forms through claims to genes or cells composing them; the Harvard distinction may thus have limited practical effect in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination inventions — requirement of a common result (unity of composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention is a combination of elements, the elements must produce something that is more than a mere sum of their individual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each element functions independently and there is no common result, the combination will not be considered an inventive composition of matter; examiners and courts look for a synergistic/common result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods and computer-implemented inventions — purposive claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Amazon.com one-click case: the Commissioner initially rejected the one-click patent as a 'business method.' Courts held that claims should be assessed against the statutory categories using purposive construction of the claims; the Federal Court found the claims disclosed a 'machine' and ordered re-examination; later appellate proceedings remanded claim construction to the Commissioner with attention to relevant art and foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the litigation the Canadian Patent Office updated examination practice (PN2013-02 and PN2013-03) implementing purposive construction and issuing guidance for computer-implemented inventions. Business methods are not categorically excluded; analysis focuses on claim construction and whether the claimed subject matter fits a statutory category when purposively construed.
